description: Cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) is a highly destructive agricultural pest widely distributed across Africa, Europe, Asia, Australia, and South America. The adult moth itself does not directly damage crops, but it lays eggs on host plants. The larvae that emerge feed on leaves, buds, flowers, fruits, and seeds of many economically important crops. Due to its high reproductive capacity and strong migratory ability, this pest can spread rapidly and produce multiple generations per year in warm climates.
symptoms: Larvae boring into fruits or pods
Damaged cotton bolls producing poor quality lint
Presence of frass and feeding tunnels in fruits or grains

life_cycle.eggs: Yellowish-white eggs laid on leaves, buds, flowers, or fruits. Eggs hatch within 3–11 days.
life_cycle.larvae: Larvae feed for 19–36 days through several instars and cause the main plant damage.
life_cycle.pupae: Pupation occurs in the soil or plant debris; pupae can overwinter in colder climates.
life_cycle.adult: Adult moths are light brown with a wingspan of about 3.5–4 cm. Adults live around 10 days and females can lay hundreds to thousands of eggs.

economic_significance: The pest causes severe yield losses in cotton, tomato, maize, chickpea, and other crops. Larvae attack reproductive plant parts and reduce yield and quality. Damage can also allow secondary fungal and bacterial infections.

monitoring: Regular field scouting for eggs and larvae
Use pheromone traps to detect adult moth activity
Monitor plant damage in buds, fruits, and flowers
cultural_control: Removal of crop residues and weeds
Deep ploughing after harvest to destroy pupae
Use of trap crops such as sunflower or marigold
mechanical_control: Handpicking and destroying eggs and larvae
Removing infested fruits and plant parts

chemical_control.note: Chemical insecticides should be used within an Integrated Pest Management strategy and only when pest populations exceed economic thresholds.
